6.2.2. Consequence-cause matching
We computed the diﬀerence in the probability ascribed to the
conspiracy theory and to the lone gunman for each participant, thereby
creating a contrast score for each. A positive score means the partici-
pants believe the conspiracy to be more likely than a lone gunman.
As shown in Fig. 3, the existence of a consequence-cause matching
bias was clearly present in the control condition (Mlarge = 14.12,
SDlarge = 28.36 vs. Msmall = −0.89, SDsmall = 42.50; t(93) = −2.06,
p < .05), but it appeared even stronger in the limited time perspective

The purpose of these comparisons was to determine if the clusters showed meaningful differences on
variables that were external to the cluster analysis. Signiﬁcance tests which meet the Bonferroni
correction (p < 0.002) are also presented in Table 2.
Demographic variables
One-way ANOVAs indicated that the groups differ in age (F(2, 164) = 3.19, p < 0.05). Post-hoc tests
showed that free agents (M ¼ 59.7) are signiﬁcantly older than satisﬁcers (M ¼ 55.2). The results of x2
tests showed group differences in gender composition (x2 ¼ 11.4, p < 0.01). Satisﬁcers had the higher
percentage of males (60.5 percent) whereas maximizers (63 percent) and free agents (78 percent) had
more women.
Work characteristics
The one-way ANOVA results showed group differences in nine out of 15 preferred work
characteristics. Satisﬁcers, free agents, and maximizers varied in their preference for part-time
work (F(2, 148) = 5.46, p < 0.01), full-time work (F(2, 149) = 5.06, p < 0.01), on-the-job training

Vision statement
The results of the analysis of covariance for the viability of the vision statements are presented in Table 3. Four covariates were
included in this analysis, including gender (F(1, 177)=1.07, p=.30), promotion regulatory focus (F(1, 177)=6.48, p≤.01), task
motivation (F(1, 177)=6.48, p≤.01), and task order (F(1, 177)=2.84, p=.09). The analysis revealed a two-way interaction be-
tween outcome framing and strategic orientation (F(1, 177)=3.81, p≤.05). Examination of the cell means indicated that visions
were most viable under balanced thinking strategies. A shift between positive outcomes and a prevention strategy focused on
avoiding failure (M=2.97, SD=.10) resulted in the most viable visions, followed by a shift between negative outcomes and a
promotion strategy for achieving success (M=2.86, SD=.10). Thinking about negative outcomes and a prevention strategy
(M=2.74, SD=.10) or positive outcomes and a promotion strategy (M=2.69, SD=.10) produced less viable visions.
The findings with regard to vision statements provided additional support for Hypothesis 1 which articulated that more viable
visions would be formulated under balanced thinking conditions. The findings also provided some support for Hypothesis 2,

conducted on the six items with orthogonal rotation (varimax). The Kaiser-
Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure verified the sampling adequacy for the analysis,
KMO = .84 (‘‘great’’ according to Field, 2009), and all KMO values for individ-
ual items were ..78 (above acceptable limit of .5 according to Field, 2009).
Bartlett’s test of sphericity, x2(15) = 8,261.23, p < .000, indicated sufficiently
large interitem correlations for PCA. A single component had an eigenvalue
above Kaiser’s criterion of 1, that explained 56.33% of the variance (thus no
rotation was obtained). The scree plot unambiguously indicated this single
component, Whanaungatanga. Internal consistency of these items as a scale
was strong, with a Cronbach’s a = .83, and the factor loadings for items were
all sufficiently strong (ranging from .65 to .8; see Table 1).
Given the degree to which these items met conventional PCA criteria as
a scale, this analysis indicates that they can be used as a reliable measure of
Te Kotahitanga’s theorized (and qualitatively validated; Bishop et al., 2007)
conception of Whanaungatanga. Taken together as a simple summative
scale (averaged), this measure obtained a reasonably normal distribution,
with a range from 1 to 5 and a mean of 3.65 (SD = .74, SE = .01). Table 2
presents the measures of skew and kurtosis obtained indicated this roughly
normal distribution (both are very slightly negative).
